destination.title: A $2 Test Turned Blue. She Served 21 Days. Police Still Carry the Kits.

candidate_payload_lines: The following year the Texas legislature passed House Bill 34, titled "An act relating to measures to prevent wrongful convictions," effective September 2017.
In August 2010, in a strip-mall parking lot in Houston, Amy Albritton watched a police officer drop a crumb from her car floor into a vial of pink liquid.
Late in the afternoon he changed lanes, and to this day she cannot say whether he signalled.
In 2010, in one of the largest police departments in America, saying what a crumb was took about ninety seconds and cost two dollars.
In a property room, in a sealed envelope, sat a crumb nobody had examined with anything more sophisticated than a colour.
The record notes something the judge never asked about: why the woman in front of her could not stop crying long enough to finish a sentence.
In 2011 a national study commissioned by the Justice Department found that prosecutors in nine out of ten jurisdictions surveyed accepted guilty pleas on nothing but the result of a field test.
Her breathalyzer reading was zero point zero.

In 1973 — the same year Richard Nixon formally created the Drug Enforcement Administration and declared, in his words, an all-out global war on the drug menace — two California inventors patented what they called a disposable comparison detector kit.
In 1974 the National Bureau of Standards studied the kits and wrote that they should not be used as sole evidence for the identification of a narcotic or drug of abuse.
The courtroom where a field test would be thrown out is a room almost nobody ever reaches.
Scott, Junior, developed it in 1973 while he was working for the DEA, and in 1990 he founded his own company.
In 2014, the last year for which records were available, Houston bought nine thousand of his kits.

On the twenty-third of February 2011, an analyst named Ahtavea Barker sat down at the Houston Police Department crime laboratory with the evidence from a traffic stop the previous August, and did what a field kit cannot do.
The scale in the laboratory measured what was left at zero point zero one three four grams.
It was six months late, and it was addressed to nobody.
Eventually managing property again, in Baton Rouge, for a landlord whose buildings nobody else wanted, at a wage that did not include an apartment.
Between January 2004 and June 2015, the office had failed to correct four hundred and sixteen variants.
era_note: Modern America. The case runs 2010-2016 in Houston, Texas, so present-day patrol cars, booking areas, county jails, courthouses and crime laboratories are correct. The origin strand (the 1973 patent, the 1974 National Bureau of Standards finding, the 1978 Justice Department conclusion) must be carried by era-neutral objects - paper files, index cards, records rooms, government corridors - never by 1970s costume staging and never by modern digital instrumentation standing in for a 1970s bench.

shorts.angle: The whole procedure that turned a crumb into a felony charge was a colour change in a two-dollar vial, and it took about ninety seconds.
shorts.avoids: This Short is only the object and the chemistry. It does not touch the plea arithmetic or the county's count of its own errors, which the other two Shorts carry.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: If the American government determined in writing in 1978 that this test proves nothing, why is it still riding in patrol cars?

shorts.angle: People who had done nothing pleaded guilty five times faster than people who really had been carrying drugs, because waiting cost them everything and bought them nothing.
shorts.avoids: This Short is only the plea arithmetic. It does not explain the kit's chemistry, and it does not reach the county's count of its own errors.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: What was sitting in a sealed envelope in the property room while she was confessing to it in open court?
shorts.loop_join: L8 names the thing as arithmetic with one answer; L1 states the result that arithmetic produces — the innocent pleading five times faster than the guilty.

lines.text: The innocent plead five times faster than the guilty. That is not a paradox; it is the system working as designed.
source_lines: The innocent plead five times faster than the guilty. That is not a paradox; it is the system working as designed.

lines.text: Investigators measured how long innocent people took to plead guilty in these cases. The median was four days.
source_lines: they measured how long it had taken those innocent people to plead guilty. The median was four days.

lines.text: Fifty-eight per cent pleaded guilty at the first opportunity, the very first time they stood in front of a judge.
source_lines: Fifty-eight per cent of them pleaded guilty at the first opportunity they had, at arraignment, the very first time they stood in front of a judge.

lines.text: Then they measured the people who really had been carrying drugs. That median was twenty-two days. Waiting bought them something.
source_lines: Then they measured the people who really had been carrying drugs. That median was twenty-two days.

lines.text: For someone innocent and poor, waiting costs everything and buys nothing, because a positive test is already in the file.
source_lines: If you are innocent and poor, waiting costs everything and buys nothing, because a positive test is already in the file and there is no laboratory report in there to argue with.

lines.text: Amy Albritton was offered forty-five days for a plea, against two years in a Texas prison if she fought and lost.
source_lines: Plead guilty, and the sentence would be forty-five days in the county jail — of which she would probably serve about half.
The maximum penalty was two years in a Texas state prison.

lines.text: She could not post bond. Her job came with her apartment. Fighting meant losing both for certain. She was sentenced to forty-five days.
source_lines: Fighting it meant staying in custody, because she could not post the bond.
She was sentenced to forty-five days. She served twenty-one.

lines.text: There is a phrase for what happened that makes it sound like a decision. It was arithmetic, and the arithmetic only has one answer.
source_lines: There is a phrase for what happened next that makes it sound like a decision. It was not a decision. It was arithmetic, and the arithmetic only has one answer.

shorts.angle: The office that won every one of those convictions went back through its own files and counted four hundred and sixteen of its own errors.
shorts.avoids: This Short is only the count and the letter. It does not explain the kit, and it does not run the plea-speed arithmetic the second Short carries.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: What happened to the hundred and seventy-two convictions that were still standing after the office finished counting?
shorts.loop_join: L8 states that the institution that convicted them is the institution that found them; L1 gives the number it found when it looked.

lines.text: Between January 2004 and June 2015, the Harris County District Attorney's office had failed to correct four hundred and sixteen variants.
source_lines: Between January 2004 and June 2015, the office had failed to correct four hundred and sixteen variants.

lines.text: A variant is a case that closed with a guilty plea, and then a laboratory report arrived saying the evidence was something else.
source_lines: A case would close with a guilty plea, and then, weeks or months later, a laboratory report would arrive saying the evidence was not what the defendant had confessed to possessing.

lines.text: Every single one had ended in a guilty plea. In two hundred and fifty-one, the laboratory finding was: no controlled substance.
source_lines: Every single one had ended in a guilty plea.
The laboratory's finding, in the office's own file, was the same three words that were on Amy Albritton's sheet. No controlled substance.

lines.text: Two hundred and twelve of those cases came from one police department. All two hundred and twelve of those people pleaded guilty.
source_lines: Of those three hundred and one, two hundred and twelve were built on evidence the laboratory determined was not a controlled substance.
All two hundred and twelve of those people pleaded guilty.

lines.text: Ninety-three per cent were sentenced to jail or prison. Fifty of them had no prior drug conviction of any kind.
source_lines: Ninety-three per cent were sentenced to jail or prison. Fifty of them had no prior drug conviction of any kind.

lines.text: One form letter went out in July 2014. It said the recipient was prosecuted for a drug offense and convicted in error.
source_lines: One of the letters had gone out on the twenty-ninth of July 2014.
accordingly, you were prosecuted for a criminal drug offense and convicted in error.

lines.text: It was posted to the address on her driver's licence — the apartment that came with the job the conviction took away.
source_lines: It was posted to the address on her driver's licence.
The letter telling Amy Albritton she had been convicted in error was mailed to the home the conviction took away from her.

lines.text: This was not uncovered by a newspaper or a federal investigation. The institution that convicted them is the institution that found them.
source_lines: Not a defence campaign, not a newspaper, not a federal investigation.
The institution that convicted them is the institution that found them.
